title: Account identifier — the canonical definition, v1
description:
THE ONE DEFINITION OF WHAT A DUDO LOGIN IDENTIFIER IS. Every contract that accepts one — login-v1, organization-onboarding-v1, organization-detail-v1, credential-reset-v1, confirmation-v1 — states this shape, and this file is the authority they state it from.

WHY IT EXISTS: it was already defined in five places and no two agreed. Measured 2026-09-05 across credential-store.ts, login-v1.schema.json, organization-onboarding-v1.schema.json, organization-detail-v1.schema.json and the two client kdf.ts copies. Three of them permitted more than one '@' and two did not; two prose descriptions of the SAME pattern disagreed with each other, and one disagreed with the pattern printed directly above it. Nothing failed, because nothing in this repository executes JSON Schema (ADR 0009) — a divergence between five hand-checked definitions is invisible until a real address falls in the gap between them.

THIS IS NOT A NEW DECISION. The restriction was decided by docs/decisions/0015 §D and has been recorded in login-v1 since it was authored. This file consolidates it; it does not narrow or widen anything, with the single exception of the '@' count noted below, which is a correction toward what Core has always done.

NOT EXECUTED. Normative and hand-checked. No validator reads it, which is exactly why one definition is worth more here than in a repository where a build would catch the drift.

accountIdentifier.description:
A Dudo login identifier — an email address, used as the account key and as the client-side PBKDF2 salt.

THE THREE RULES, WHICH ARE credential-store.ts::isSubmittableIdentifier's AND ARE TRANSCRIBED RATHER THAN INVENTED:
  1. Length 3 to 254 inclusive. 3 is the shortest thing that can be an address ('a@b'); 254 is below RFC 5321's 256-octet path cap, and every byte past it is work an unauthenticated caller can compel on the hashing path.
  2. Every character in U+0021..U+007E — printable ASCII. SPACE (U+0020) IS EXCLUDED with the whole control range and everything above U+007E.
  3. AT LEAST ONE '@'. Not exactly one.

RULE 3 IS A CORRECTION, MADE 2026-09-05, AND IT IS THE ONE PLACE THIS FILE CHANGES SOMETHING. organization-onboarding-v1 and organization-detail-v1 both carried the pattern ^[!-?A-~]*@[!-?A-~]*$, whose character classes are U+0021..U+003F and U+0041..U+007E — printable ASCII with '@' (U+0040) REMOVED — so it permits EXACTLY ONE '@'. Core has never required that: isSubmittableIdentifier sets a boolean when it sees an '@' and never counts them. So those two contracts were STRICTER THAN THE RUNNING CODE, and the prose above each pattern disagreed — onboarding's said 'at least one', detail's said 'exactly one', over identical patterns encoding 'exactly one'.

THE CORRECTION GOES TOWARD CORE, AND IT IS ALSO THE MORE CORRECT READING OF THE STANDARD: RFC 5321 permits a quoted local part containing '@', so "a@b"@example.com is a legal address that the exactly-one pattern refuses. Widening an accepted value set is ADDITIVE under API_STANDARD.md §6; narrowing Core to match the stricter pattern would have been breaking and would have refused legal addresses for no security gain.

WHAT THIS PATTERN DOES NOT DO: it is DELIBERATELY NOT AN EMAIL VALIDATOR. It does not decide whether an address is deliverable — nothing in Dudo sends mail — and a stricter grammar would refuse valid addresses for no security gain. It decides exactly one thing: whether every implementation of normalizeIdentifier will agree, byte for byte, on the normalised form.

CLIENTS MUST NOT TRIM. A value needing whitespace removed is REFUSED, never repaired, because JavaScript's trim() and Swift's trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines) remove different character sets — so a value that needs trimming is a value the implementations can disagree about. A client may refuse such input in its own UI before sending; it must not silently alter what it sends, because the value it sends becomes the KDF salt.

normalizedAccountIdentifier.description:
The result of applying normalizeIdentifier to an accountIdentifier: NFKC, then ASCII-ONLY case folding (U+0041..U+005A mapped down by 32, and nothing else). It is the PBKDF2 salt and the input to the HMAC lookup hash.

IT NEVER APPEARS ON ANY WIRE, IN EITHER DIRECTION, IN ANY DUDO CONTRACT. It is defined here because it is the value both clients must compute identically, and a shape nobody can inspect is still a shape both implementations have to agree on. The pattern encodes 'printable ASCII with no uppercase A-Z', which is what ASCII-only folding guarantees for an input already constrained to printable ASCII.

IT IS NOT toLowerCase() AND NOT lowercased(). Those are full Unicode case mapping and they differ between JavaScript and Swift for real characters — U+0130 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER I WITH DOT ABOVE is the standard example. On Apple the correct call for the NFKC step is precomposedStringWithCompatibilityMapping, which is one word away from precomposedStringWithCanonicalMapping (NFC, which is the PASSWORD's rule, not this one).

NFKC IS THE IDENTITY FUNCTION OVER THE ACCEPTED INPUT SET. Every accountIdentifier is printable ASCII, and NFKC changes no ASCII character. The step is applied anyway so the definition stays correct if the ASCII restriction is ever relaxed by a recorded decision, and so all implementations already agree on the step rather than adding it under pressure later.
